conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand how you’re doing so we can give you the best support possible. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go at your pace, one question at a time, and it usually takes just a few minutes.

To begin: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, it’s been kind of hard. I can still chuckle at a cute meme or something my partner says, but most of the time I feel too tired and low to really laugh. So I’d say it’s been more difficult than it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yeah… like if my husband makes a goofy face at the baby I’ll catch myself giggling, but it feels kind of forced and fades fast. Most of the time the heaviness is still there, so it’s definitely harder than before she was born.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really… even little things I used to get excited about—like my favorite show dropping a new episode—feel kind of flat. I still go through the motions, but it’s like the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing her right or I ate something that upset her through the breast milk. A couple of nights ago she wouldn’t settle and I kept replaying everything I’d done—was it the coffee I had at lunch, did I hold her wrong, am I just not cut out for this? Logically I know babies cry, but the guilt still crashes in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my chest feels tight, wondering if her breathing sounds different or if the blanket’s too close to her face. Then my mind jumps to “what if she stops breathing tonight?” and I can’t shake it for a while. There’s always this low-level buzz that something bad could happen even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it spikes into a real wave of panic—like last night when she stirred in the bassinet, my heart started racing and I felt short-of-breath, sure something awful was happening even though she was just rooting. It usually passes after a few minutes, but in that moment it feels huge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. Between feedings, diapers, trying to grab a bite myself, and the house piling up, I get this heavy “I can’t keep up” feeling. I manage to push through because I have to, but I’m constantly overwhelmed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—worrying I missed something, replaying every little sound she made, wondering if I’m doing any of this right—and then I’m wide-awake for an hour or two. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake at every tiny noise, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that pretty much sums up most of my days. I wake up with this heavy, gray feeling that sticks around. I’ll look at her little face and feel love, but it’s like there’s a rain cloud sitting on top of it. I keep waiting for it to lift, but it hasn’t yet.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve broken down twice this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and I felt like my body was failing her, and again yesterday when my mom left after dropping off groceries. The tears just came and I couldn’t stop them. It’s not all-day sobbing, but when it hits, it feels like the dam bursts.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It flashed through my mind a couple of times—like when I was rocking her at 3 a.m. and everything felt hopeless, I had this fleeting picture of just disappearing. I don’t want to die and I’d never leave her, but for a second the thought of not feeling this awful seemed like relief. There’s no plan or anything, just those quick, scary moments.

I hear how heavy life feels right now: the joy of your baby is real, yet most moments are clouded by sadness, relentless worry, and a sense that you're failing even when you're doing your best. The exhaustion, racing thoughts at night, and waves of guilt are wearing you down, and fleeting thoughts of disappearing show how overwhelmed you feel.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, fleeting laughter that feels forced, indicating a clear reduction in ability to enjoy humor.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes loss of enjoyment even for previously pleasurable activities and absence of excitement, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('do that a lot', 'immediately think it's because I'm not soothing her right', 'guilt still crashes in') matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive worries about infant safety without real danger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic episodes that occur "sometimes," matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling constantly overwhelmed, barely treading water, and unable to keep up most days, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly trouble falling and staying asleep linked to unhappiness and racing worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, pervasive sadness that dominates most days and has not lifted, aligning with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct episodes of uncontrollable crying triggered by specific stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated, distressing thoughts of disappearing during hopelessness, fitting "Sometimes" even without active suicidal intent.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 26 far exceeds the 14 threshold for probable major depression. Patient endorses majority of <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest (<quote>the spark isn't there</quote>), guilt (<quote>guilt still crashes in</quote>), fatigue, insomnia, and recurrent passive suicidal ideation (<quote>thought of just disappearing</quote>). Anxiety symptoms are prominent yet mood symptoms predominate. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent referral to GP, psychiatrist, or perinatal mental-health team
2. Ensure continuous adult support for you and baby until review
3. Develop a written safety plan including 24-hour crisis contacts
4. Encourage 20-minute rest windows once daily; reduce non-essential tasks
5. Offer evidence-based therapy options (CBT, IPT, or mother-infant units)
6. Discuss medication compatible with breastfeeding if clinically indicated
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS within one week to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Summary Note

Patient-reported symptoms cluster around:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness (Q2, Q8, Q9)
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Daily, intrusive anxiety and episodic panic without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm and sense of inability to cope (Q6)
- Initial insomnia and fragmented sleep related to ruminative worry (Q7)
- Fleeting passive suicidal ideation without intent or plan (Q10)

Pattern consistent with elevated risk for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety. Safety concern noted due to presence of self-harm ideation; immediate safety assessment and referral for comprehensive evaluation recommended.
